blurb: The one everyone pictures, but the garden varieties open into a hundred soft petals instead of the tight cone you get at a corner shop.

imageAttribution.title: Rosa hybrida, Yellow, Rosier serie Flower Carpet, Jardin universitaire Roger-Van den Hende 30.jpg

blurb: Arrives as a hard ball and opens over three days into something absurd. Season is short and everyone wants them, which is most of the price.
Petals laid out in a spiral so precise it looks engineered. Comes in everything from a golf ball to a dinner plate.
Layer after layer of petals as thin as tissue, on a stem that curves wherever it likes. The florist favourite that never photographs as well as it looks.

imageAttribution.title: Persian buttercup - Ranunculus asiaticus var. albus.jpg

blurb: Keeps growing after you cut it and leans toward the nearest window, so an arrangement rearranges itself overnight.
The scent fills a room within an hour, which people either love or find is a bit much. Pollen stains, so florists pinch the anthers off.
A single face big enough to carry a whole jar on its own. Reads as friendly rather than romantic, which is sometimes exactly right.
One stem fills a third of a vase. The colour depends on soil pH, which is why the blue ones look faintly unreal.
The size of a grapefruit and closer to an artichoke than a rose. Dries beautifully, so it outlasts everything else in the vase by months.
A jet-black centre against a pale petal — the highest-contrast thing you can put in a bouquet without it looking loud.
A perfect flat circle of colour. Cheap, available year round, and slightly divisive — some people find it a bit cartoonish.
Unfashionable for a decade and quietly back, especially the big spidery ones. Lasts nearly three weeks in water.
Four trumpets on one hollow stem, each the width of your hand. Florists stuff the stem with a bamboo cane so it can hold its own head up.
One clean curve and nothing else. Three of them in a tall vase is a complete arrangement — anything more starts to fight it.

imageAttribution.title: Calla lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica), Parque do Monteiro-Mor, Lisbon, Portugal julesvernex2.jpg

blurb: Falls like velvet with a fuzzy stripe down the middle. Lasts about three days, which is the price of looking like a Van Gogh.
Reads as a rose from across the room and costs a third as much. Each stem carries several blooms plus buds, so it keeps opening.
Crumpled like it was folded in a pocket, on a hairy stem that wanders. Florists sear the cut end so it doesn't bleed out.

imageAttribution.title: Iceland Poppy Papaver nudicaule 'Champagne Bubbles' Pink Flower.jpg
imageAttribution.artist: Photo by and (c)2008 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man). Co-attribution must be given to the Chanticleer Garden.

blurb: A metre of flowers opening bottom to top over a week. Divisive — some read it as grand, some as funeral parlour.
One of the very few genuinely blue flowers, which is why it costs what it does. Gives an arrangement height without weight.
Pinch the side of a bloom and it opens like a mouth. The tips curve upward in the vase no matter which way you set them.
Smells like cloves and cinnamon from across the room. Cheap, generous, and does most of the scent work in a spring bouquet.
Delphinium's looser cousin — the same blue spires but thinner, so it scatters through a bouquet instead of anchoring it.
A one-sided tower of speckled thimbles. Genuinely poisonous, so it belongs in a vase and nowhere near a kitchen counter.

imageAttribution.title: Bloemen en knoppen van Vingerhoedskruid (Digitalis purpurea). Locatie, Tuinreservaat Jonkervallei 01.jpg

blurb: A dense cone of pea-shaped flowers stacked in tiers. Reads as meadow rather than florist, even in a formal vase.
The best-smelling thing in the flower market and the shortest-lived — four days if you are lucky. Worth it anyway.
Blooms march along one side of an arched stem and open in sequence. The scent is the citrus-and-honey one used in half of all soap.

imageAttribution.title: 香雪蘭(小蒼蘭) Freesia refracta -香港花展 Hong Kong Flower Show- (9255262036).jpg

blurb: Written off for thirty years and now everywhere again, mostly in the odd antique shades. Lasts two weeks and smells faintly of cloves.
Freckled throat, six blooms per stem, and it will outlast every other flower in the vase. The reliable middle of most mixed bunches.
The sap poisons other flowers, so it needs to sit in its own water overnight before joining a mixed arrangement.
A fat column of waxy stars on a stem that is basically all water. The scent is enormous for the size of the flower.

imageAttribution.title: Garden Hyacinth Hyacinthus orientalis 'Blue Jacket' Flower 2000px.jpg

blurb: Barely fifteen centimetres tall and the most saturated blue in the market. Used in tight clusters where the eye needs somewhere to land.
Tiny nodding bells with a scent completely out of proportion to their size. Priced like a luxury because the season is three weeks long.
A flat disc of petals on a wire-thin stem, so it floats above everything else and moves when you walk past.

imageAttribution.title: Cosmos bipinnatus in Jardin universitaire Roger-Van den Hende, Quebec city, Quebec, Canada.jpg

blurb: The colours are frankly unsubtle, which is the point. Straight from a cutting garden rather than a wholesaler.
A tight ball of ruffles in a gold that borders on radioactive. The foliage smells sharp and green when you handle it.

imageAttribution.title: Tagetes erecta Marigold flower at Madhurawada 01.JPG

blurb: A domed pincushion on a stem thin enough to nod. The seed heads left behind are arguably better than the flower.
Sits inside a haze of thread-fine foliage, which is where the name comes from. Adds fog to a bouquet rather than colour.
A fringed blue button on a grey-green stem. One of the few blues that costs almost nothing.

imageAttribution.title: Centaurea cyanus or Cornflower in the gardens of Darjeeling Tourist Lodge.jpg

blurb: Flat-topped clusters of small fringed flowers, often two-toned with a pale eye. Reads as texture from a distance.

imageAttribution.title: Sweet William - Dianthus barbatus, Finzel Swamp, Finzel, Maryland, June 29, 2020.jpg

blurb: Flat plates of hundreds of tiny flowers on a ferny stem. Dries in place without dropping, so it just quietly stays.
Petals sweep back off a bristly copper cone, so it reads as a shuttlecock more than a daisy.

imageAttribution.title: Echinacea purpurea, Jardín Botánico, Múnich, Alemania, 2013-09-08, DD 01.jpg

blurb: Gold petals around a near-black dome. The cheapest way to get real contrast into a warm arrangement.

imageAttribution.title: "Rudbeckia hirta" Black-eyed Susan Gibberd Garden Essex England (cropped).JPG

blurb: Dozens of small daisies on one branching stem, arriving right as everything else in the garden gives up.
A pincushion sitting inside a papery collar of pointed bracts. Looks like something pressed in a book a century ago.
A perfect sphere of hundreds of tiny stars on a bare stem. Faintly oniony up close, because it is one.
A yellow drumstick on a leafless stem. Completely dries out and stays exactly the same, indefinitely.

imageAttribution.title: Pycnosorus globosus plant1 (17361585844).jpg
imageAttribution.artist: Harry Rose from South West Rocks, Australia

blurb: Thin tapering spires that curve at the tip. Gives a bouquet vertical lines without the weight of a delphinium.
Either a velvet brain or a flame, depending on the type. The texture is genuinely unlike anything else available.
A papery clover-shaped button that feels dry to the touch even when fresh. Scatters small points of colour through a mix.
A single flat heart that looks wet and plastic even when it is not. Lasts three weeks and reads entirely as design object.
An orange crest and a blue tongue emerging sideways from a beak-shaped bract. Impossible to make look soft.
A cylinder of thousands of hooked filaments in tight rows. Australian, alien-looking, and effectively permanent once dried.
Faces downward and flowers in the cold, in colours that all look slightly dusty. The most grown-up flower on this list.

imageAttribution.title: Helleborus orientalis, Zaaddozen zwellen, Locatie, Tuinreservaat Jonkervallei 01.jpg

blurb: Petals arranged in near-perfect concentric rings against very dark glossy leaves. Drops the whole flower at once when done.
Sold as a bare branch that opens indoors over a week. Gives an arrangement height and negative space at the same time.

imageAttribution.title: Prunus serrulata Kanzan blossom Jardin des Plantes 2013-04-21.jpg

blurb: Enormous scented cones on a woody stem. Wilts fast unless the stem end is split, and is worth the trouble for about five days.
Thick waxy white petals that bruise brown if you touch them. The scent is enormous and unmistakable.
Comes on a trailing vine, so it drapes over the edge of a vase instead of standing up in it.
Cone and collar both stiff, spined, and a metallic blue that looks almost painted on. Sharp — literally.
A perfect steel-blue sphere bristling all over. Half geometry lesson, half weapon.

imageAttribution.title: Azurite - Echinops ritro - 2 - par Mickael Schauli.jpg

blurb: Waxy white flowers up a tall spike with a scent so heavy it is used as a perfume base note on its own.

imageAttribution.title: Polianthes tuberosa, Burdwan, West Bengal, India 10 01 2013.jpg

blurb: A dozen flat faces marching up an arching stem. Lasts two to three weeks, which is unusual for something this delicate-looking.
Thick waxy blooms the size of a palm, often in greens and browns you would not expect from an orchid.
Clusters of narrow four-pointed tubes. Fine-textured enough to soften the edge between a big focal flower and greenery.
The flower a child draws. White ray petals, gold centre, no complications whatsoever.
Petals swept fully backward with wavy edges, red fading to gold. Looks mid-motion even sitting still.
Narrow curling petals that catch light like they have glitter in them, which is an actual property of the cell structure.
An exploding sphere of trumpets on a bare stem — the airy, open version of what an allium does densely.

imageAttribution.title: 2026 Agapanthus africanus. Santiago de Compostela. Galiza.jpg

blurb: Domed heads of flat five-petalled flowers, often with a contrasting eye. Smells like the middle of July.
A dome of curved styles shooting outward like a frozen firework. Structural enough to carry an arrangement alone.
Small waxy white trumpets, traditionally wired individually into bridal work. Heavy jasmine scent.
A small egg-shaped head that ripens from green to wine, on a stem that bends wherever it likes.

imageAttribution.title: Gebarsten bloemknop van een Kogellook (Allium sphaerocephalon) 15-05-2022. (d.j.b) 02.jpg

blurb: Domed lace-caps in a green so pale it goes cream at the edges. Softens hard-edged flowers better than any greenery.
Five or six small roses per stem instead of one large one. Fills the gap between a focal rose and a filler.
Simple open faces on tall wiry stems that never stop moving. Nothing like the bold coronaria anemone despite the name.
Opens deep coral and fades to peach then near-cream over four days, so the same stem is three colours across its life.

imageAttribution.title: Paeonia 'Coral Charm' 5 2021 xPeony- (51208163914).jpg
imageAttribution.artist: F. D. Richards from Clinton, MI

blurb: Sold as a cut branch with leaves like polished leather. One stem is an entire arrangement.
A two-metre spire of crepe-paper saucers opening bottom to top. Pure cottage garden.
Enormous cupped petals on a bare stem. The seed pods left behind are a florist staple in their own right.
Long scented racemes that hang straight down. Cut branches last only days, which is rather the point.
Great domed trusses on a woody branch, backed by dark evergreen leaves.

imageAttribution.title: Rhododendron Petticoat lane. (20342657866).jpg
imageAttribution.artist: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand

blurb: A row of little lockets strung along an arching stem. Nothing else in a spring bouquet looks like it.
Nodding bonnets with long backward spurs, on stems fine enough to tremble.

imageAttribution.title: Columbine Aquilegia vulgaris 'Black Barlow' Flower 2000px.jpg
imageAttribution.artist: Photo by and (c)2008 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man). Co-attribution must be given to the Chanticleer Garden.

blurb: Flat gold discs on sticky, resinous stems that smell sharply green when you cut them.
Small gold daisies with fringed tips, held high on wiry stems that move in any draught.
Dense violet spires on square stems that smell herbal when handled. Reliable vertical line.
Flat heads of tiny purple flowers that smell strongly of vanilla and cherry pie.

imageAttribution.title: Close-up of heliotrope flower (Heliotropium arborescens), Jardim da Fundação Calouste Gulbenkian, Lisbon, Portugal julesvernex2.jpg

blurb: The bracts are genuinely papery and rustle when touched. Dries without changing at all.
A velvety orange disc on a hollow stem that has to be handled carefully — it bends where you grip it.
Clusters in scorched oranges and browns, with a scent somewhere between violet and clove.
The first thing to flower, often through frost. Sold in small tied posies rather than by the stem.
Nodding bells up one side of an arching stem. The cultivated Spanish kind, not the protected native.

imageAttribution.title: Hyacinthoides non-scripta, bastaard van Hyacinthoides hispanica. Boshyacint. d.j.b. 05.jpg

blurb: Sold in tight nosegays with their own leaves as a collar. The scent famously switches itself off as you smell it.
